argument: Friedrich Hayek argued that centrally planned economies, however well-intentioned, are doomed because no planner, however smart, can ever match the dispersed 'localized knowledge' held by millions of individual market participants, and because prices, not government fiat, are what convey true information about supply, demand, and value. Beyond being unworkable, Hayek argued central planning is actively dangerous: it concentrates enormous power in the hands of a few, tends to elevate the most ruthless people to that power, and puts societies on 'the road to serfdom' toward totalitarianism.
keyIdeas: Hayek argues a complete understanding of how to structure an economy is fundamentally unknowable, not just difficult: 'how little they really know about what they imagine they can design.'
Like language, economic order emerges spontaneously from the aggregated choices of many people and cannot be designed all at once by a central authority.

No centralized body can match an individual's 'localized knowledge' of their own corner of the economy, illustrated by Grandma Beatrice's flower shop, and without market prices planners have no reliable way to know a resource's true value.

A society can't have both equality of outcome and equality under the law: treating people fairly and identically under the law lets their different choices lead to different outcomes, so guaranteeing equal outcomes requires treating people unequally.

Centrally planned power structures tend to elevate the most ruthless, ambitious people to positions of control ('Why the Worst Get on Top'), putting societies on the 'road to serfdom' toward totalitarianism.

terms.def: A government-directed economy in which a central body plans and controls production and distribution instead of relying on markets.
The dispersed, fragmented knowledge individual participants (like a shop owner) hold about their own corner of the economy, which no central planner can fully access.
The idea that systems like language and the economy self-organize from the aggregated choices of many people rather than top-down design.
Hayek's claim that central planning of the economy is the first step on a path toward totalitarianism.
